Course 03 — Scalable Data Science

Does El Niño
reach Saudi Arabia?

Can a phenomenon 17,000 kilometres away leave a measurable fingerprint on the climate here? Five cities, twenty-five years, over a million records.

Ritaj  ·  AI & Data Science Diploma
Tuwaiq Academy  ·  Riyadh
01 — Mechanism

What is
El Niño?

El Niño is one phase of ENSO. The equatorial Pacific warms, and that warming reorganises the winds, the humidity and the atmospheric circulation far beyond the ocean itself.

When an effect travels that far from where it started, we call it a teleconnection. That is the entire premise of this project.

El Niño · warm phase

Trade winds weaken

Warm water spreads east across the basin. Convection follows it, and circulation reorganises worldwide.

La Niña · cool phase

Trade winds strengthen

Upwelling intensifies, the cold tongue widens westward, and the pattern flips its sign almost everywhere it reaches.

02 — Data

Three sources,
one million records.

ERA5Reanalysis fields — temperature, humidity, windECMWF
NASA POWERSurface meteorology and solar variables per siteNASA
NOAA RONIRelative Oceanic Niño Index — the ENSO predictorNOAA CPC

RONI rather than ONI, deliberately: it measures the Niño 3.4 anomaly relative to the tropical mean, so a warming background doesn't get mistaken for an ENSO event.

A random split would let the model read tomorrow's weather out of next year's data. Walk-forward validation only ever trains on the past and tests on the future — the same constraint a real forecaster works under.

04 — Before the model

Finding
data leakage.

The first results were excellent. That was the warning sign. Three separate leaks were inflating accuracy, and each one had to go before any model was trained.

Leak 01

Global climatology

A single global baseline let the model learn the seasonal cycle instead of the departure from it.

Leak 02

ET₀

Reference evapotranspiration is derived from temperature — so a predictor was quietly carrying the target inside it.

Leak 03

Time-of-day pattern

The diurnal temperature signature let the model recover the hour, and the hour gave away the answer.

Every one of them raised accuracy artificially. None of them would have survived contact with real forecasting.

04 — Before the model

From temperature
to anomaly.

Rather than let the model discover that summers are hot and afternoons are hotter, I computed a climatology for every city, month and hour, then predicted the departure from it.

The target, restated·
How hot was it?
How far from normal was it?
Same data. A far harder,
and far more honest, question.
05 — Results

Temperature:
no clear signal.

I started with temperature, and the result was unambiguous — ENSO alone carried no useful predictive information about temperature anomalies in any of the five cities.

This is not a model that failed. It is evidence that ENSO's influence on Saudi temperature is marginal next to local and regional drivers.

Temperature anomalyResult
No usable
ENSO signal Local and regional drivers dominate
A bounded negative result. It tells
the next researcher where not to look.
05 — Results

Rainfall:
the signal appears.

Moving to rainfall changed everything. Rain days were roughly 1.68 times more frequent during El Niño than during La Niña.

Which raised the question that turned out to matter most: when does this effect actually show up?

Rain-day frequencySignal
1.68× El Niño compared with La Niña
El Niño1.68×
La Niña1.00×
06 — The surprise

Why autumn,
not winter?

Winter is our wettest season. But autumn turned out to be the season most sensitive to El Niño — the ratio there reached 2.41×.

Autumn is also when the largest shifts in water vapour and southerly winds appear, which may be what gives the signal its strength.

Seasonal sensitivityAutumn
2.41× Rain-day ratio, autumn
Wettest ≠ most sensitive.
The season with the most rain is not
the season ENSO moves the most.
07 — Refinement

Canonical
vs. Modoki.

El Niño is not one thing. In a Canonical event the warming concentrates in the eastern Pacific; in a Modoki event it sits closer to the centre of the basin.

Where the warming sits changes where the winds shift — and therefore which regions feel it.

Canonical

Eastern Pacific

Maximum anomaly toward South America. The textbook event.

Modoki

Central Pacific

Peak near the dateline, flanked by cooler water on both sides.

Warming centreCANONICAL
160°EDateline80°W
Watch the globe: the anomaly slides west
and cool lobes open on either side.
07 — Refinement

One country,
different responses.

Saudi Arabia does not behave as a single region. The west responded more strongly to Canonical events, while the centre and east responded more to Modoki.

West
Stronger response to Canonical
Centre & East
Stronger response to Modoki

Averaging the country into one number would have hidden the entire story.

08 — Timing

The signal
arrives early.

The timing of the response also varies by city. Some regions showed the signal early, and some responses extended to three months.

That points to a seasonal early indicator — not a forecast of whether it will rain on a given day. The distinction matters, and I want to be clear about it.

Response lead timeUp to 3 months
Lag 1 month·
Lag 2 months·
Lag 3 months·
Seasonal signal, not daily prediction.
09 — Takeaway

A different fingerprint
on every city.

Temperature

No clear ENSO signal

Local and regional drivers dominate. A bounded, reportable negative result.

Rainfall

1.68× more rain days

El Niño compared with La Niña — a real and detectable effect.

Season

Autumn, at 2.41×

Not the wettest season. The most sensitive one.

Geography

Response varies by city

West leans Canonical, centre and east lean Modoki, with lags up to three months.

A phenomenon that begins thousands of kilometres away can leave a different fingerprint on every city in Saudi Arabia — which is exactly why a national average would have told us nothing.

End

Thank you.

Questions welcome — especially about the leakage, which is the part I learned the most from.
